stimulus.text: Alexander Hamilton, Report on Public Credit, January 1790: “A national debt, if it is not excessive, will be to us a national blessing.” Paraphrase: Hamilton proposed that the federal government pay the national debt at full value and take over the states’ war debts, funding both by selling government bonds.
stimulus.source_note: Alexander Hamilton, Report on Public Credit, January 1790. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quotes Hamilton, Report on Public Credit, January 1790, public domain.

primary_sources: Alexander Hamilton, Report on Public Credit (January 1790)

stem: According to Hamilton, why would paying the national debt at full value be a “national blessing”?

options.text: It would let the government stop collecting taxes altogether.
options.misconception: Paying the debt did not mean taxes would end.

options.text: It would show lenders the new government paid what it owed.
It would move the nation’s capital to the Potomac River.
options.misconception: The capital bargain was separate from the debt plan and its purpose.

options.text: It would give the states full control over the nation’s money.
options.misconception: Hamilton’s plan strengthened the national government, not the states.

rationales.B: Background: paying the debt in full would prove the new government kept its promises, so lenders would trust it and lend again.
rationales.A: Background: Hamilton funded the debt with bonds and new taxes, so the plan did not end taxation.
rationales.C: Background: the capital’s site came from a separate bargain, not from the debt plan itself.
rationales.D: Hamilton’s plan put the debt under the national government, not under the states.
rationales.general:
1. Hamilton calls the national debt a “national blessing” when it is properly funded.
2. Background: a government that pays its debts in full earns lenders’ trust, and trust is what lets it borrow again.
3. The stimulus shows Hamilton tying the debt to the government’s standing, not to ending taxes or moving the capital.
4. So the “blessing” is credit: a government known to pay its debts can borrow when it needs to.
Remember: when a leader calls a debt a blessing, look for the trust it builds, not the money it costs.
